explanations.action-of-6-july-1746--battle-of-madras-: Both articles state the same mechanism and neither of them states it as a sequence of dates. The Madras article's background: “After fighting an inconclusive battle the two fleets withdrew to repair, with the British retreating to Ceylon and the French using their base at Pondicherry. Wary of fighting another major naval battle – the British commander, Edward Peyton, chose to stay away from the Coramandel coast and withdrew to the safety of Bengal, leaving the British settlements on the Coramandel badly exposed to the French. The French Governor of Pondicherry Dupleix authorised an attack on Madras.” The action's own article says the other half: “La Bourdonnais acquired additional guns at Pondicherry, and when the fleets met again in August 1746, Peyton refused battle and retreated to Bengal. La Bourdonnais then proceeded to lead the successful French attack on Madras in September.” An indecisive engagement that sent one fleet to Bengal and left the other repairing and rearming at Pondicherry is what left Madras open from the sea; `enabled` rather than `caused`, because the decision to attack was Dupleix's and the article says so in the same paragraph. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.action-of-9-february-1799-south-africa--: The February article closes on exactly this link: "In the Indian Ocean theatre the loss of Prudente was compounded a few weeks later by the capture of Forte at the action of 28 February 1799, which left Sercey with a shortage of available warships. At the action of 11 December 1799 his last frigate, Preneuse, was intercepted and destroyed off Île de France." The Port Louis article says the same from its own side — "the squadron dispersed in 1798 and by the summer of 1799 Preneuse was the only significant French warship remaining in the region" — and it is that solitude, not any order given in February, that put one frigate against a blockading ship of the line. Precondition-of: a stated reduction in force, not a cause of the December action.
explanations.american-revolutionary-war--french-revol: The French Revolution's own article, at the revision this atlas cites for that record, says: **"At the same time, the American Revolution and the European revolts of the 1780s inspired public debate on issues such as patriotism, liberty, equality, and democracy."** The sentence names the American Revolution, the broader movement; this atlas holds its armed phase, which the war's own article calls **"the final eight years of the broader American Revolution"** (revision 1376266742). That identification is the one step this edge takes beyond the article, and it is why the type is `inspired` and the confidence `probable`: the sentence names an inspiration among others and asserts no more.
explanations.american-revolutionary-war--inconfidenci: The Inconfidência's own article, which this atlas already cites for the record, opens by naming its cause in so many words: **"It was the result of a confluence of external and internal causes. The external inspiration was the independence of thirteen British colonies in North America following the American Revolutionary War"**. The article says inspiration and the atlas has a type for that, so `inspired` is the type and not `caused`: the sentence puts the internal causes beside the external one and does not rank them. Probable, for the reason every edge drawn from this source is.
explanations.american-revolutionary-war--treaty-of-pa: The treaty's own article opens by naming what it was: **"The Treaty of Paris, signed by representatives of King George III of Great Britain and representatives of the United States on September 3, 1783, officially ended the War of American Independence and recognized the Thirteen Colonies … to be free, sovereign, and independent unified states."** The war's own article says the same from the other end — the victory at Yorktown **"led King George III and the Kingdom of Great Britain to negotiate an end to the war"** (revision 1376266742). A settlement that a war is negotiated into is caused by it, so the type is `caused`; `probable`, for the reason every edge drawn from this source is. The treaty is also *part of* the war here, which is a display fact and not an argument — `parent` does not enter the adjacency, so this edge is what puts the treaty in the graph at all.
explanations.anglo-french-war-1778-1783--battle-of-fo: Fort Royal's article names the war it belongs to rather than the American one: "a naval battle fought off Fort Royal, Martinique in the West Indies during the Anglo-French War on 29 April 1781, between fleets of the British Royal Navy and the French Navy." Enabled: the Anglo-French war is what put two fleets off Martinique.
explanations.anglo-french-war-1778-1783--estates-gene: The umbrella this edge crosses is the point of it (A15 (11)): France’s war and the assembly that was called to pay for it sit under different parents and the atlas held no link between them. The Anglo-French War article, at revision 1370901054, states the consequence twice — “The cost of participation in the American war inexorably led to France’s own bankruptcy six years later, setting the stage for the French Revolution”, and “over 1.3 billion livres had been spent over the five year conflict … the debt caused major economic and political problems and, as the country struggled to pay its debts, this eventually led to the Financial Crisis of 1786 and ultimately to the French Revolution in 1789”. The Estates General article, at revision 1375588196, arrives at the same sum from the other side — “As a result of the financial support given to the Americans during the war against Great Britain, the amount totaled 1.25 billion livres, and France was heavily in debt” — and its own lead says what the assembly was for: “The assembly was a desperate attempt to resolve a catastrophic fiscal crisis.” A15 (5) decides the `from` end: the sentences name the cost of France’s own participation, which in this atlas is the Anglo-French War and not the American war it was fought inside, so the edge is written from that record. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: a debt is not a summons. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.anglo-french-war-1778-1783--invasion-of-: Dominica's own article makes France's entry into the war the thing that set the invasion going, and dates it: "The action took place before British authorities in the Caribbean were aware that France had entered the war as an ally of the United States of America. The French governor in the West Indies, Francois Claude Amour, marquis de Bouille, was notified on 17 August that France was at war, and organized the invasion." Enabled and not caused: the war is what made the attack possible and gave de Bouille his orders, not what decided that Dominica in particular would be taken.
explanations.anglo-french-war-1778-1783--spain-and-th: Spain came in through France and the article says so in its first sentence: "Spain, through its alliance with France and as part of the Anglo-French War (1778-1783) with Britain, played an important role in the independence of the United States. Spain declared war on Britain as an ally of France, itself an ally of the American colonies." Enabled and not caused: the alliance is the route in, and the article does not claim France obliged Spain to declare.
explanations.bali-strait-incident--battle-of-port-lou: Both articles state the same mechanism from their own side: the squadron that was sent to the Indian Ocean in 1796 came apart after its two failures, which is why by 1799 one frigate was left to be caught. The Port Louis article: "Sercey deployed his squadron to the Dutch East Indies, but suffered frustration at the action of 9 September 1796 and the Bali Strait Incident of January 1797 and subsequently returned to the base at Port Louis. There the squadron began to fracture, with a succession of ships sent back to France or detached on independent missions." The Bali Strait article, from the other end: "Sercey retired with his frigates to Île de France, where he learned to his horror of the opportunity he had missed in the Bali Strait. His squadron required extensive repairs, but the Colonial Committee on Île de France remained rebellious over attempts to abolish slavery and denied his ships men and food supplies. Eventually Sercey was forced to disband his squadron, sending four frigates back to France." Precondition-of: the dispersal is what left Preneuse alone, and neither article says the incident compelled the December 1799 cruise.
explanations.bali-strait-incident--macau-incident-179: The later article names the earlier one as the first of two attempts on the same thing by the same force: “the allied squadron attempting to disrupt a valuable British merchant convoy due to sail from Qing Dynasty China. This was the second such attempt in three years; at the Bali Strait Incident of 1797 a French frigate squadron had declined to engage six East Indiamen on their way to China.” Its background says why there was a second: “Sercey's force had subsequently broken up as it proved too expensive to maintain as a cohesive force … Sercey decided to augment his forces by uniting them with the allied Spanish squadron at Manila.” Two attempts by one admiral's squadron on one annual convoy is a campaign and not a date order, which is the footing batch 38's series edges stood on. What the article does **not** say is that the first attempt produced the second, and this edge does not say it either: `precondition-of`, because the 1797 failure is what left the China Fleet still sailing and Sercey still hunting it, and the decision to try again with Spanish help was taken for the reasons the background gives. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.bali-strait-incident--raid-on-manila--pr: The Manila article gives the raid its reason and names the incident as what put the question: "In January 1797 the convoy had been attacked by the French squadron in the East Indies, comprising six frigates commanded by Contre-amiral Pierre César Charles de Sercey. In the ensuing Bali Strait Incident the commander deceived Sercey into believing that the unescorted convoy contained disguised ships of the line and the French admiral retreated, only learning of his error on his return to Île de France. There was considerable concern in India that Sercey might try again in 1798, or that the Spanish, who maintained a powerful squadron at Cavite, might make an attempt of their own." That concern is what sent Rainier's escorted convoy to China and put Cooke at Macau, from where he "decided to investigate the state of readiness of Spanish forces in Manila himself". Precondition-of and not caused: the article gives Cooke's own curiosity and the rumoured treasure ship as the immediate reasons for the raid, and the incident as the standing danger the escort answered.
explanations.battle-of-bennington--battles-of-saratog: Bennington is in this atlas because of what it took away from Burgoyne rather than what it decided on the day. The Bennington article, at revision 1375222856, states the consequence and names the record this edge runs to: “it reduced Burgoyne’s army in size by almost 1,000 men, led his Native American allies to largely abandon him, and deprived him of much-needed supplies, such as mounts for his cavalry regiments, draft animals and provisions, all factors that contributed to Burgoyne’s eventual defeat at Saratoga.” The type is `enabled` and not `caused` because “factors that contributed to” is what the article claims and no more: the detachment Stark destroyed had been sent out to forage, and its loss is a condition of the September and October defeat rather than the thing that produced it. The Saratoga article, at revision 1377478794, is the second reading, putting Burgoyne’s surrender at the second of the two battles. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-bunker-hill--new-york-and-new-: Both articles put the decision to go for New York on what Bunker Hill had cost, and both state it as a cause rather than as a sequence. The campaign article, at revision 1370629551, gives the decision and who took it: “They defeated Patriot forces in the Battle of Bunker Hill, suffering very high casualties. When news of this expensive British victory reached London, General William Howe and Lord George Germain, the British official responsible, determined that a ‘decisive action’ should be taken against New York City using forces recruited from throughout the British Empire as well as troops hired from small German states.” The Bunker Hill article, at revision 1375011142, says the same thing from the other end: “The battle led the British to adopt a more cautious planning and maneuver execution in future engagements, which was evident in the subsequent New York and New Jersey campaign. The costly engagement also convinced the British of the need to hire substantial numbers of Hessian auxiliaries to bolster their strength in the face of the new and formidable Continental Army.” The two agree on both halves — the target and the German troops — which is why this is `caused` and not `inspired`: the campaign is what the expensive victory was answered with. A15 (5) is satisfied without substitution, because the campaign is the event the campaign article's own sentence names. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-camden--battle-of-cowpens--rea: Cowpens was fought the way it was because of what the militia had done at Camden, and both articles state that as a cause and not as a sequence. The Camden article, at revision 1376333498, says what followed from the defeat: “Following the battle, Morgan revised the southern army’s use of militia and won a decisive victory at the Battle of Cowpens on January 17, 1781.” The Cowpens article, at revision 1376280446, names the failure being answered and the answer: “the Battle of Camden had ended in disaster when the militia, which comprised half of the American force, broke and ran as soon as the fighting started, leaving the American flank exposed. To eliminate that possibility, he defied convention by placing his army between the Broad and Pacolet rivers.” “To eliminate that possibility” is why this is `reacted-to` rather than chronology: the same article’s “Coming in the wake of the American defeat at Camden, Cowpens was a surprising victory” states only an order of events and is refused under A15 (5). Read in the atlas’s direction, `A reacted-to B` says B answered A. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-cartagena-de-indias--invasion-: The Cuba article makes the defeat at Cartagena the reason for the invasion, in one sentence: "Vernon had made an unsuccessful attempt to capture Cartagena in 1741, and after his repulse he directed the fragments of his sickly and dispirited followers against the island of Cuba." The same section says the force was the same force: "The land forces consisted of the remnants of the troops from Cartagena, some 3,000 British and American troops". `caused`: the article does not merely date one after the other, it says the repulse is what sent Vernon to Cuba and what the army he landed was made of. Probable, and with a second author: the sentence is cited there to Pares, War and Trade in the West Indies, pp. 91-92.
explanations.battle-of-cowpens--battle-of-guilford-co: The Cowpens article, at revision 1376280446, ends its account with the consequence in one clause: “Morgan evaded Cornwallis and joined American General Nathanael Greene’s army near Greensboro, North Carolina, in early February, resulting in the Battle of Guilford Court House.” The Guilford article, at revision 1376260995, opens its background on the same fact from the British side — “On 18 January 1781 Lord Cornwallis learned he had lost one-quarter of his army at the Battle of Cowpens. Yet he was still determined to pursue General Nathanael Greene into North Carolina and destroy Greene’s army” — so the pursuit that brought on the March battle is the one the loss of the light troops set going. `caused` and not `enabled`, because “resulting in” is what the article says. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-fontenoy--battle-of-melle--pre: The Melle article opens on what Fontenoy left behind: "After their defeat at Fontenoy in May, the Duke of Cumberland, Allied commander in Flanders, was under pressure from the Austrians to defend Brussels. He also wanted to protect the key port of Ghent, a major supply depot threatened by the French advance into West Flanders." The defeat is not given as the cause of the encounter — the column marched for Ghent — but it is the position Cumberland was fighting from, which is what precondition-of says. The lead carries no citation of its own.
explanations.battle-of-fort-charlotte--siege-of-pensa: Both articles make Mobile the precondition of Pensacola, in their own words and not this atlas's. “Battle of Fort Charlotte”, revision 1374387321: “Their capitulation secured the western shore of Mobile Bay and opened the way for Spanish operations against Pensacola”, and, of the fort's fall, “it drove the British from the western reaches of West Florida and reduced the British military presence in West Florida to its capital, Pensacola”. “Siege of Pensacola”, revision 1374389510, says the same from the other end: “Gálvez began planning an assault on Pensacola, West Florida's capital, using forces from Havana with the recently captured Mobile as the launching point for the attack”. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the siege was delayed a year by British reinforcements and by Solano's hurricane, which is the same article's account, so Mobile is what made Pensacola possible and not what brought it about. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-fort-washington--battle-of-tre: The other half of the Long Island article's sentence, at revision 1370268460: “Howe defeated Washington in battle again at White Plains and then again at Fort Washington. Because of these defeats, Washington and the army retreated across New Jersey and into Pennsylvania.” The Fort Washington article, at revision 1377296439, is the second author and states it from its own end in its § Aftermath: “Three days after the fall of Fort Washington, the Patriots abandoned Fort Lee. Washington and the army retreated through New Jersey and crossed the Delaware River into Pennsylvania northwest of Trenton, pursued as far as New Brunswick, New Jersey, by British forces. After about one month, on the night of December 25–26, 1776, Washington crossed the Delaware and defeated the Hessian garrison under the command of Rall at Trenton.” Taken alone the second passage is a sequence; taken with the first, which says “because of”, it is the same claim stated twice. `precondition-of`, for the reason the White Plains edge beside it gives. `probable`, on the articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-grand-turk--treaty-of-paris-17: The last British attempt on the islands failed and the peace decided them instead: "Although the mission failed, the islands were restored to Britain in the second Treaty of Paris that formally concluded the war six months later." Precondition-of: the treaty settles what the action could not.
explanations.battle-of-guilford-court-house--siege-of: This is the link that joins the southern campaign to a record the atlas already held. The Guilford article, at revision 1376260995, states it: “Later, Cornwallis chose to march into Virginia and attempt to link with roughly 3,500 men under British Major General Phillips and Brigadier General Benedict Arnold. These decisions allowed Greene to unravel British control of the South, while leading Cornwallis to Yorktown, where he was forced to surrender to General George Washington and French Lieutenant General Comte de Rochambeau.” The Camden article, at revision 1376333498, is the second reading and is the plainer of the two about why the march happened: “At the Battle of Guildford Court House in March 15, 1781, Cornwallis won a tactical victory against Greene but suffered heavy casualties, which led the British general to march to Virginia and unite with a larger army there, ultimately resulting in the decisive Franco-American victory in the Yorktown campaign.” The casualties are the battle’s own, which is why the edge is written from the battle and not from the decisions the Guilford sentence makes its subject; A15 (5) would send it elsewhere only if those decisions were themselves a record this atlas holds, and they are not. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-harlem-heights--battle-of-whit: The check at Harlem Heights is why Howe stopped pushing north up Manhattan and went round instead, and the flanking movement is what brought both armies to White Plains. The Fort Washington article, at revision 1377296439, states the turn in one sentence in its § Movements: “His northward progress was checked the next day in the Battle of Harlem Heights, after which he sought to flank the strong U.S. position on the north of the island. After an abortive landing attempt on October 11, Howe began landing troops in southern Westchester County, New York (in today's The Bronx) on October 18, intending to cut off the Continental Army's avenue of retreat. Washington, aware of the danger, withdrew most of his troops north to White Plains.” The White Plains article, at revision 1374379337, is the second author and tells it the same way in its § Background: “Howe followed up with a landing on Manhattan on September 15, but his advance was checked the next day at Harlem Heights. After an abortive landing at Throg's Neck, he landed troops with some resistance at Pell's Point on October 18 to begin an encircling maneuver that was intended to trap Washington's army.” `precondition-of` and not `caused`, because the immediate cause of a battle at White Plains is the encircling manoeuvre and the lightly held supply depot there, and this atlas holds neither Throg's Neck nor Pell's Point: what Harlem Heights supplied was the reason Howe was flanking at all. `probable`, on the articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-ile-ronde--bali-strait-inciden: The Île Ronde article states that the failed blockade was never renewed and what filled the gap: "With Renaud's squadron still at Port Louis, Rainier considered renewing the blockade, but was dissuaded by the dangers of the monsoon season and a false report that a squadron of French ships of the line was soon due to arrive on Isle de France. In 1795 he was distracted by the sudden need to guard against the Dutch East India colonies following the French conquest of the Netherlands, and he supervised the invasion of Ceylon and operations against the Dutch East Indies. By the time his attention turned once more to Isle de France, it had been heavily reinforced in early 1796 by a frigate squadron commanded by Counter-admiral Pierre César Charles de Sercey." The Bali Strait article names the same squadron and the same reason for sending it: "In response to British activity in the region and the reluctance of the inhabitants of Île de France to follow orders from the National Convention abolishing slavery, the French dispatched a squadron of frigates to the East Indies early in 1796." Precondition-of: the island left unblockaded is what Sercey's squadron could be based on, and neither article says the 1794 action brought on the encounter of January 1797.
explanations.battle-of-la-guaira--battle-of-puerto-ca: The La Guaira article states the condition and names the other record while doing it: "97 of Knowles' men were killed, among whom was the captain of HMS Burford, and many of the ships were badly damaged or lost. Knowles was therefore unable to proceed to Puerto Cabello until he had refitted." Its own account of the days after says the same: Knowles "decided to retire to west before sunrise on 6 March and attack nearby Puerto Cabello", and went to sea again on 31 March "once his main body had been refitted". `precondition-of`: the damaged squadron is the state the April attack was mounted from, and "therefore" is the article's word. Probable, and on Wikipedia alone: the sentence is cited to "The Navy In the War of 1739-48", Cambridge University Press, p. 251, which the article names without an author, a year or an identifier.
explanations.battle-of-lauffeld--siege-of-maastricht-: The Lauffeld article states it in so many words: "Lauffeld was thus another French victory that failed to achieve a decisive result, although it led to the capture of Bergen-op-Zoom in September and Maastricht in May 1748." The paragraph closes on a citation to Anderson, p. 211. "Led to" over ten months is a claim about what was made possible and not about what followed directly, so the type is enabled. The same sentence states the same of Bergen op Zoom, and that edge could not be written: the atlas dates that siege to July 1747 at month precision and Lauffeld to 2 July, which rule 4 reads as an arrow pointing backwards.
explanations.battle-of-long-island--battle-of-harlem-: Harlem Heights was fought on Manhattan because Long Island had put the Continental Army there, and both articles state that mechanism rather than the order of the two battles. The Harlem Heights article, at revision 1375220259, opens its § Background with it: “On August 27, 1776, British troops under the command of General William Howe flanked and defeated the American army at the Battle of Brooklyn. Howe moved his forces and pinned the Americans down at Brooklyn Heights, with the East River to the American rear. On the night of August 29, General George Washington, Commander-in-Chief of the Continental Army, evacuated his entire army of 9,000 men and their equipment across the water to Manhattan.” The article's own link behind “Battle of Brooklyn” is the Battle of Long Island, so the event named is the battle this atlas holds. The Fort Washington article, at revision 1377296439, is the second author and states the British half of the same turn in its § Movements: “After first gaining control of western Long Island in the Battle of Long Island at the end of August 1776, British General William Howe launched an invasion of Manhattan on September 15. His northward progress was checked the next day in the Battle of Harlem Heights.” The type is `precondition-of` and not `caused` because neither article says the defeat produced the engagement of 16 September — what it produced was an army on Manhattan and a British army following it there. `probable`, on the articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-long-island--battle-of-trenton: This is the condition Trenton was a gamble against, and it is deliberately not the same claim as the campaign-level edge beside it. The Trenton article, at revision 1377458911, names Long Island by name in its § Background: “In early December 1776, American morale was incredibly low. The Americans had been ousted from New York by the British and their Hessian auxiliaries, and the Continental Army was forced to retreat across New Jersey. Ninety percent of the Continental Army soldiers who had served at Long Island were gone. Men had deserted, feeling that the cause for independence was lost.” “Ousted from New York” carries the article's own link to the Battle of Long Island, so the event this sentence names is the battle. What the sentence states is the state the army was in, not the decision to attack — the decision the same article puts on the campaign as a whole — so the type here is `precondition-of` and not `caused`: Long Island is what left the army needing Trenton, and the campaign is what produced it. **One article carries this and not two**: the Long Island article, at revision 1370268460, attributes the retreat across New Jersey to White Plains and Fort Washington (“Because of these defeats, Washington and the army retreated across New Jersey and into Pennsylvania”) and not to Long Island, so it is not a second author for this claim and is not cited as one. `probable`, on the one article (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-melle--fall-of-ghent--enabled: The Ghent article states the connection as a count of men: "A column of 4,000 to 5,000 British, Hanoverian, Dutch and Austrian reinforcements sent by the Duke of Cumberland was defeated by the French at the Battle of Melle with only some 1,000 men getting through to Ghent." Melle is what kept the garrison from being reinforced, so the town fell to a force it could otherwise have met. The sentence carries no footnote of its own; the citation two sentences later (Skrine, 1906) is attached to a different claim, so it is not named here.
explanations.battle-of-mollwitz--siege-of-brieg--enab: The Brieg article puts the two in one sentence: "When the Prussians defeated the Austrian relief army at the Battle of Mollwitz on 10 April 1741, the garrison of Brzeg (Brieg) was doomed. After a few weeks, the Austrian garrison surrendered and was allowed free passage to the fortress of Nysa (Neisse)." Mollwitz did not take the town; it removed the army that could have relieved it, which is what enabled means here. The lead carries no citation of its own, so Wikipedia is the only author named and the confidence stays probable.
explanations.battle-of-negapatam-1782--battle-of-trin: This is the one link in the series for which the article gives a mechanism and not only an order. Trincomalee “was the fourth in a series of battles fought between the two fleets off the coast of the Indian subcontinent”, and the article says what put Suffren there: “Suffren and Hughes then met a third time off Negapatam, again with inconclusive results, after which Suffren anchored off Cuddalore to make repairs”, and then — “Due to the exposed nature of the anchorage at Cuddalore, and the impending arrival of additional British fleets, Suffren decided to attempt the capture of Trincomalee to gain a safe harbour for his fleet where he might effect more substantial repairs.” An indecisive battle that left him repairing in an exposed roadstead is why he went for the harbour; `precondition-of` rather than `caused`, because the decision was Suffren's and the article gives him two reasons of which Negapatam is one. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-pfaffenhofen--treaty-of-fussen: The treaty article names the battle as the thing that decided it: "When Charles VII died in Munich on 20 January 1745, his successor as Elector of Bavaria, Maximilian III Joseph, signed a preliminary peace with Austria. But a strong war-party led by Ignaz von Törring and supported by France wanted to continue the war. After the decisive defeat in the Battle of Pfaffenhofen on 15 April, Maximilian Joseph chose for peace." The Pfaffenhofen article says the same from the other end — the war-party leader was dismissed the day after and the treaty was concluded a week later. Neither passage carries a footnote, so Wikipedia is the only author named.
explanations.battle-of-pillpinto--siege-of-cusco-1781: Two sentences of the article, and the edge is no wider than what stands between them. The first groups this battle with two others as the victories the rising's first phase turned on: **"This initial phase of the rebellion in Cusco and the south was marked by key victories, such as the capture of Ayaviri, the Battle of Pillpinto, and especially the Battle of Sangarará, which consolidated rebel control over the Cusco region."** The second gives the offensive against Cusco as the attempt to keep what had been won: **"Seeking to maintain the advantages gained at Quiquijana, Sangarará, and Lampa, he decided to anticipate the enemy and go on the offensive."** **The second sentence does not name Pillpinto**, and this record says so rather than reading it in: what the article supports is that Pillpinto is one of the victories that made the position the offensive set out from, which is `enabled` at `probable` and nothing stronger. Pillpinto's own article adds what was held there — "a small women's brigade led by Tomasa Tito Condemayta successfully suppressing the Spanish militia from capturing Túpac Amaru II" (revision 1370586073).
explanations.battle-of-porto-bello-1739--battle-of-ca: The Porto Bello article argues the larger expedition out of this victory: "Vernon became a popular hero in the wake of the victory and was promoted to the rank of admiral. He had been one of the advocates of a more belligerent approach towards Britain's enemies even prior to this expedition, and after the victory, British Prime Minister Robert Walpole was under great pressure by the Opposition to launch similar raids along the Spanish coast. Vernon's next battle in this campaign, a large-scale invasion of Cartagena in 1741, ended in defeat." `enabled`: the acclaim and the political pressure it made are what the article says put Vernon in front of Cartagena, and it claims no more than that. Probable, and on Wikipedia alone at one revision: the sentence about Cartagena is footnoted to Victoria 2005 with the article's own {{Page needed}} tag on it, so there is no locator to carry a second author, and the Marley the article cites elsewhere is its 1998 first edition, not the 2008 one this atlas holds.
explanations.battle-of-providien--battle-of-negapatam: The third of the same five, which the Negapatam article says of itself — “the third in a series of battles fought between a British fleet, under Vice-Admiral Sir Edward Hughes, and a French fleet, under the Bailli de Suffren” — and which it reaches through the second in as many words: “After both fleets spent time in port repairing, refitting, and re-provisioning, they met again in the April Battle of Providien, south of the Ceylonese port of Trincomalee, that was ended by a storm and then nightfall.” The repairs are why the two fleets were apart for three months and the series is why they met again; `probable`, Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-sadras--battle-of-providien--p: The two articles number themselves in one series. Sadras “was the first of five largely indecisive naval battles fought between a British fleet (under Vice-Admiral Sir Edward Hughes) and a French fleet (under Admiral Pierre Suffren) off the east coast of India during the Anglo-French War”; Providien “was the second in a series of naval battles fought between” the same two fleets and the same two admirals. An ordered series named as one by both of its members is a claim about the campaign, not a date order: `precondition-of`, and `probable` because Wikipedia states the sequence and no mechanism between these two.
explanations.battle-of-sangarara--siege-of-cusco-1781: The rebellion's article, opening its "Siege of Cusco" section, gives the march on the city as a decision taken to hold what had been won: **"Seeking to maintain the advantages gained at Quiquijana, Sangarará, and Lampa, he decided to anticipate the enemy and go on the offensive."** The sentences on either side put the same thing in order — Túpac Amaru returned to Tungasuca on 17 December, "the rebel leader began preparations for the great expedition against Cusco", and the army departed on 20 December. `enabled` and not `caused`, because Sangarará is one of three advantages the sentence names and the article gives no weight to any of them; what the source supports is that the victory was part of the position from which the offensive was launched, and not that it brought the offensive about.
explanations.battle-of-santiago-de-cuba-1748--battle-: The Havana article sets the cruise against the Santiago failure and links to it: "In April 1747 Admiral Sir Charles Henry Knowles had become commander in chief on the Jamaica station but had failed to subdue Santiago de Cuba the following year. After having his ships had refitted at Port Royal Knowles sailed on a cruise in search of Spanish treasure convoys hoping to intercept the Spanish treasure fleet off Cuba." The refit is the one the Santiago article accounts for, where two ships of the line "were put out of action by the batteries of Morro Castle and had to be towed to open sea". `precondition-of` and nothing stronger: the article's "but" is an argument about what Knowles had to show for the station, not a claim that the failure brought the October action about. Probable, on Wikipedia alone at one revision.
explanations.battle-of-saylla--siege-of-cusco-1781--p: The article puts the two engagements two days apart and in one sequence: the reinforcements under Avilés entered Cusco on 1 January 1781, then **"On 2 January, alerted by the priest of Urcos, the cavalry of the Royalists, commanded by Joaquín de Varcárcel and Francisco Laisequilla, destroyed Castelo's vanguard in the town of Saylla, killing 400 rebels and capturing a flag bearing the coat of arms of Túpac Amaru"**, and then **"On 4 January, Túpac Amaru ordered his troops to move around the city"**, which is where the siege begins. **The article gives the order and the position and states no cause between them**, which is why the type is the weakest one the arrangement supports and the confidence is `probable`: the royalist cavalry had broken the rebel vanguard outside the city before the main army reached it, and that is the whole of what is claimed here. (Saylla's own article dates the action 3 January; the rebellion's dates it 2 January. Neither is preferred here and the record keeps its item's own date.)
explanations.battle-of-shubra-khit--battle-of-the-pyr: The later article gives the mechanism and not only the fortnight between them: “On 13 July, French scouts located Murad's encampment near Shubra Khit. Bonaparte ordered an immediate advance, leading to the skirmish at Shubra Khit (also called Chobrakit). French artillery destroyed the Mamluk flagship on the Nile and **forced a retreat**, giving Bonaparte his first victory and demonstrating the effectiveness of concentrated firepower against cavalry charges.” The Mamluk army that fell back from Shubra Khit is the army the French met again at Embabeh eight days later, and the divisional square the French formed there is the tactic the article says Shubra Khit proved. `precondition-of`: the first engagement did not cause the second, it set the field and the method of it. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-st-lucia--capture-of-st-lucia-: The naval action is what kept the island's garrison from being relieved: "During the Battle of St. Lucia, the British fleet defeated a French fleet sent to reinforce the island... Realising that another British fleet would soon arrive with reinforcements, the French garrison surrendered." Precondition-of: the surrender follows from the reinforcement having been stopped, which is what the battle did.
explanations.battle-of-the-assunpink-creek--battle-of: Cornwallis deciding to finish the Assunpink Creek attack in the morning is what let Washington leave in the night, and Princeton is where he went. The Assunpink Creek article, at revision 1371410210, states both halves in its lead: “After assaulting the American positions three times and being repulsed each time, Cornwallis decided to wait and finish the battle the next day. Washington moved his army around Cornwallis's camp that night and attacked Mawhood at Princeton the next day.” The Princeton article, at revision 1375498890, is the second author and reads it the same way in its lead: “On the night of January 2, 1777, Washington repulsed a British attack at the Battle of the Assunpink Creek. That night, he evacuated his position, circled General Cornwallis' army, and attacked the British garrison at Princeton.” `enabled` and not `caused`: the decision to attack Princeton was Washington's and the article attributes it to him, but the opening he took it through was the stalemate at the creek. `probable`, on the articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-the-chesapeake--siege-of-yorkt: The fleet action decided what the siege could be. The Chesapeake article, at revision 1370598769: “The strategically decisive battle prevented the Royal Navy from reinforcing or evacuating the besieged British army of Lieutenant-general Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia. With its victory, the French navy was able to gain control over local sea lanes and provided the Franco-American besiegers with siege artillery and troops reinforcements. These proved decisive in securing Cornwallis’ surrender.” The Yorktown article states it from the other end at revision 1376522207: “As a result of this victory, de Grasse blocked any reinforcement or escape by sea for Cornwallis and also disembarked the heavy siege guns required by the allied land forces.” `enabled` and not `caused`: the siege was already being marched to — Washington and Rochambeau arrived on 28 September — and what the battle decided was that it could be pressed and not relieved. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-the-nile--revolt-of-cairo--pre: The later article names the Nile among the reasons the French position was weak when the city rose: “The French army's situation was critical – the British were threatening French control of Egypt after their victory at the Battle of the Nile, Murad Bey and his army were still in the field in Upper Egypt, and the generals Menou and Dugua were only just able to maintain control of Lower Egypt. The Egyptians had common cause with those rising against the French in Cairo – the whole region was in revolt.” This is the weakest of the batch's edges and the explanation says so: the article states the Nile as part of a critical situation and not as the thing that produced the rising, and the sentence does turn on “after”. What keeps it out of the chronology refusal is the clause that follows it — the French could not hold Egypt against the British *and* Murad Bey *and* the city at once, which is a state of affairs and not an order of dates. `precondition-of`, never `caused`. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-the-pyramids--revolt-of-cairo-: The earlier article states the consequence and the later one what was revolted against. The Pyramids: “The victory opened the way to Cairo, where Napoleon established a new administration, though local uprisings soon followed.” The Revolt: “In 1798, Napoleon led the French Revolutionary Army's Army of the Orient in an invasion of Egypt, swiftly capturing and occupying Alexandria and Cairo. However, in October of that year, discontent against the French led to an uprising by the people of Cairo.” What the two together state is that the battle put the French administration into Cairo and the rising was against that administration; `precondition-of` rather than `caused`, because what the Revolt article names as the cause is the discontent, and the battle is what there was to be discontented with. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-the-saintes--battle-of-the-mon: The Mona Passage was the pursuit of what the Saintes had scattered: "A British fleet under Rear-Admiral of the Blue Sir Samuel Hood engaged a French squadron under Georges-Francois de Framond which had escaped the Battle of the Saintes a week earlier... completing the British victory at the Saintes." Precondition-of: the ships Hood took were the ships that got away nine days before.
explanations.battle-of-trenton--battle-of-the-assunpi: The second battle at Trenton was the British answer to the first, and the Princeton article, at revision 1375498890, says so in those words in its § Victories at Trenton: “In response to the loss at Trenton, General Cornwallis left New York City and reassembled a British force of more than 9,000 at Princeton to oppose Washington. Leaving 1,200 men under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Mawhood at Princeton, Cornwallis left Princeton on January 2 in command of 8,000 men to attack Washington's army of 6,000 troops … After three failed attempts to cross the bridge over the Assunpink Creek, beyond which were the primary American defenses, Cornwallis called off the attack until the next day.” The Assunpink Creek article, at revision 1371410210, is the second author and states the American expectation of the same reaction in its lead: “Following the victory at the Battle of Trenton early in the morning of December 26, 1776, General George Washington of the Continental Army and his war council expected a strong British counterattack. Washington and the council decided to meet this attack in Trenton and established a defensive position south of the Assunpink Creek.” The type is `reacted-to` because that is exactly what both articles describe — a force assembled and marched in response to a defeat — and the edge runs forward in time, from the defeat to the answer to it. `probable`, on the articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-trincomalee--battle-of-cuddalo: The last of the five Sadras counts — “the first of five largely indecisive naval battles” between Hughes and Suffren — and the Cuddalore article says it closed them: it “took place right before the Treaty of Paris that ended the American Revolutionary War”, and “Peace had already been agreed upon in Europe, but that news had yet to reach India, making this the final battle of the war.” **What the Cuddalore article gives as its own cause is not Trincomalee** but Hyder Ali's death — “Following the December 1782 death of French ally Hyder Ali, the ruler of Mysore and previous controller of Cuddalore, British commanders at Madras decided to attempt the recapture of Cuddalore” — so this edge carries the series and nothing more, which is what `precondition-of` and `probable` say. The atlas holds no record for Hyder Ali's death; when it does, that is the edge into this battle.
explanations.battle-of-white-plains--battle-of-fort-w: Fort Washington fell with 1,200 men in it because the army it belonged to had gone north to White Plains. The Fort Washington article, at revision 1377296439, puts the two in one breath in its § Movements: “Washington, aware of the danger, withdrew most of his troops north to White Plains. He left a garrison of 1,200 men at Fort Washington under the command of Colonel Robert Magaw, although this force was inadequate to fully defend the extensive works in hindsight.” The White Plains article, at revision 1374379337, is the second author and states the British side of it in its § Aftermath: “Howe chose not to follow, instead attempting without success to draw Washington out. On November 5, he turned his army south to finish evicting Continental Army troops from Manhattan, a task he accomplished with the November 16 Battle of Fort Washington.” So both the garrison's weakness and Howe's choice of target are traced to White Plains and what followed it. `precondition-of`, because what White Plains produced was the situation Fort Washington was lost in and not the assault itself. `probable`, on the articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-white-plains--battle-of-trento: The Long Island article, at revision 1370268460, names this battle as one of the two defeats that drove the retreat Trenton was launched from, and it does so with a cause and not a date: “Although American troops delivered an unexpected check to the British at Harlem Heights in mid-September, Howe defeated Washington in battle again at White Plains and then again at Fort Washington. Because of these defeats, Washington and the army retreated across New Jersey and into Pennsylvania.” “These defeats” is White Plains and Fort Washington, so this atlas writes the sentence as two edges rather than one. The White Plains article, at revision 1374379337, is the second author and carries the same chain to its end in its § Aftermath: “Later, British movements chased him across New Jersey and into Pennsylvania, and the British established a chain of outposts across New Jersey. Washington, seeing an opportunity for a victory to boost the nation's morale, crossed the Delaware and surprised Rall's troops in the December 26 Battle of Trenton.” `precondition-of`: the defeat put the army where Trenton was possible and made a victory necessary, and the decision to cross is the campaign's, which the atlas already holds as a separate edge. `probable`, on the articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battles-of-lexington-and-concord--siege-: The siege was the answer to the day of 19 April. The Lexington article, at revision 1376384213, states what the militias did with the retreat rather than merely when: “The militias then blockaded the narrow land accesses to Charlestown and Boston, starting the siege of Boston.” The Boston article, at revision 1377282932, gives the response in its own words — “All of the New England colonies raised militias in response to this alarm and sent them to Boston” — and that “in response to” is why this is `reacted-to` and not chronology: the same article’s other sentence, “The siege began on April 19 after the Revolutionary War’s first battles at Lexington and Concord”, states only an order of events and is refused under A15 (5). Read in the atlas’s direction, `A reacted-to B` says B answered A, so the battles stand at the `from` end and the siege at the `to`. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battles-of-saratoga--anglo-french-war-17: Both articles state the cause and not the order. Saratoga’s own lead, at revision 1377478794: “The outcome greatly affected the course of the war, persuading France to enter the war as an American ally”, and, quoting Edmund Morgan, that Saratoga “won for Americans the foreign assistance from France, which was the last element needed for victory”. The Anglo-French War article, at revision 1370901054, says the same thing from the French end and dates it: “Within days of the news of Burgoyne’s surrender reaching France, King Louis XVI decided to enter into negotiations with the Americans that resulted in a formal Franco-American alliance and the French entry into the war, moving the conflict onto a global stage.” `caused` rather than `enabled`: the decision is attributed to the news of the surrender, not merely made possible by it. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22) — the second cites Ketchum 1997, which nobody here has opened.
explanations.capture-of-alexandria-1798--battle-of-sh: The later article's background is the march out of the captured port: “The French troops then marched on and assaulted Alexandria and captured it after its Wali, Koraim Pasha, refused to surrender. After capturing Alexandria, Napoleon sent a column eastwards to capture Rosetta … The main column of the French army was hurriedly marched out of Alexandria after a rest of less than two days, ordered by Napoleon to march some 50 miles across mostly barren terrain, aiming for Ramaniyah, a village on the banks of the Nile”, and its lead places the battle “on their march to Cairo”. The Pyramids article says the same thing in one sentence: “After landing in Ottoman-controlled Egypt and capturing Alexandria on 2 July 1798, the French army under General Bonaparte marched across the desert toward Cairo.” `precondition-of` and not `caused`: Alexandria is the base the march was launched from and the supply line that made it possible, not the reason Murad Bey stood at Shubra Khit. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.capture-of-alexandria-1798--battle-of-th: The later article says why the French fleet was where Nelson found it: “With the French army ashore, Brueys' fleet anchored in Aboukir Bay, 20 miles (32 km) northeast of Alexandria. Brueys believed that he had established a formidable defensive position. The British fleet arrived off Egypt on 1 August and discovered Brueys' dispositions, and Nelson ordered an immediate attack.” The landing that took Alexandria is what put the fleet at anchor twenty miles along the same coast with its crews ashore foraging — the article's own explanation of why Brueys had “not organized reconnaissance”. `precondition-of`: the disembarkation made the anchorage necessary; Nelson's arrival is what made it a battle. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.capture-of-ayaviri--siege-of-cusco-1781-: The same two sentences, on the same reading and with the same limit. The article names the capture among the first phase's key victories — **"such as the capture of Ayaviri, the Battle of Pillpinto, and especially the Battle of Sangarará, which consolidated rebel control over the Cusco region"** — and gives the march on Cusco as the move to hold the advantages gained: **"Seeking to maintain the advantages gained at Quiquijana, Sangarará, and Lampa, he decided to anticipate the enemy and go on the offensive."** **Ayaviri is not among the three that second sentence names either.** Ayaviri's own article says what the town was taken for — "part of Túpac Amaru II's plan to expand in the Lake Titicaca and possibly unite with the rebels in Charcas" (revision 1370608267) — which is a plan and points south rather than at Cusco, and is quoted here rather than made into an edge of its own. `enabled` at `probable`, for the same reason as Pillpinto.
explanations.capture-of-fort-bute--battle-of-baton-ro: A15 (5) put this edge here. The quote that would have run from Spain's entry to Baton Rouge — “first the attack and capture of Fort Bute at Manchac, and then forcing the surrender of Baton Rouge, Natchez and Mobile in 1779 and 1780”, “Spain and the American Revolutionary War” at revision 1373209544 — names Fort Bute as what came first, so under A15 (5) the edge is written from Fort Bute or not at all. The Baton Rouge article, at revision 1370433595, states the connection rather than the order: “The six who escaped capture made their way to Baton Rouge to notify the British troops there of the fort's capture”, and the same section explains why Baton Rouge was the real battle — “Dickson had decided weeks earlier that Fort Bute, built in 1766 and in ruins, was not defensible, and had placed most of his troops at Baton Rouge”. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: taking the ruined post opened the river road and warned the garrison, it did not decide the siege. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.capture-of-grenada-1779--battle-of-grena: The sea battle was fought over what the landing had just done: "A British fleet led by Admiral John Byron had sailed in an attempt to relieve Grenada, which French forces under Charles Henri Hector, Count of Estaing had just captured." Precondition-of: without the capture there is nothing for Byron to sail to relieve.
explanations.execution-of-louis-xvi--insurrection-of-: The insurrection’s lead says what the deputies were attacked for: “Jean-Paul Marat led the attack on the representatives in the National Convention, who in January had voted against the execution of King Louis XVI and since then had paralyzed the convention.” The vote of January 1793 is the execution this atlas holds as a record, and the article gives it as the mark against the twenty-two Girondins the Commune demanded be brought before the Revolutionary Tribunal. So the later event is a reaction to the earlier one in the article’s own telling, which is what `reacted-to` says; the edge runs from the execution to the insurrection because that is the direction this atlas writes a reaction in. `probable`: the lead reports the grievance, it does not argue the causation, and rule 22 refuses `consensus` on a Wikipedia citation.
explanations.flight-to-varennes--champ-de-mars-massac: The massacre’s own lead lays the sequence out in three sentences and in this order: “two days before, the National Constituent Assembly issued a decree that King Louis XVI would retain his throne under a constitutional monarchy. This decision came after Louis and his family had unsuccessfully tried to flee France in the Flight to Varennes the month before. Later that day, leaders of the republicans in France rallied against this decision.” The article therefore makes the flight the thing the decree answered and the decree the thing the crowd came out against; what it does not say is that the flight caused the killing, and the type is `precondition-of` rather than `caused` for exactly that reason — the decree stands between them and this atlas does not hold it as a record. `probable`, on one encyclopaedia lead.
explanations.french-invasion-of-egypt-and-syria--maca: The later article states it in one clause, and it is the reason this edge exists rather than the one batch 40 refused: “However Fox and Carysfort were detached with a local convoy in November 1798, and **Rainier, whose forces were largely committed to the Red Sea following the recent French invasion of Egypt**, gave urgent orders for the frigates to be replaced by the 38-gun HMS Virginie and 74-gun HMS Arrogant.” Batch 40 withdrew the raid on Manila because the only text reaching Macau named a third event as the cause and the atlas did not hold it; the third event was this one, and A15(5) says such an edge is written from that event or not at all. It is written from that event. `enabled`: the invasion did not make the Franco-Spanish squadron sail, it took the Royal Navy squadron that would otherwise have been covering the China Fleet and put it in the Red Sea. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.french-revolution--action-of-31-july-179: The article's background puts the whole chain in one place: "The French Navy was in a state of upheaval due to the social consequences of the French Revolution, and as a result found itself at a disadvantage to the Royal Navy, which had been preparing for war since June 1792. In response, the French sent several frigate squadrons to sea, including their newest ships and best sailors and officers in an attempt to disrupt British commerce in the early stages of the war. One such squadron was sent in April 1793 to the United States, carrying the French ambassador to the United States, Edmond-Charles Genêt. After the ambassador disembarked, the squadron, under the command of Captain Jean-Baptiste-François Bompart, dispersed to raid British shipping along the coast." Precondition of, not caused: the Revolution is why a French frigate squadron was raiding off the American seaboard at all, and so why Bompart's Embuscade was lying in New York for Courtenay to challenge — but the challenge and the engagement are the two captains' own, and the article claims nothing more for the Revolution than the state of the navy that put the ship there.
explanations.french-revolution--battle-of-ile-ronde--: The Île Ronde article gives the revolution in France as the state the colony and its squadron were in, and names the decree that made it so: "Isle de France had been in a state of turmoil since the French Revolution and in 1792 the republican faction in the colony seized control. In 1794 suspected royalists were arrested, including naval officer Armand de Saint-Félix, their executions forestalled by the arrival of news that the French Convention had abolished slavery. Only the intervention of Governor Anne Joseph Hippolyte de Maurès, Comte de Malartic prevented unrest. The preoccupation of the naval authorities had prevented any offensive operations and the reduced squadron, now commanded by Captain Jean-Marie Renaud, remained in Port Louis." The same two conditions are what put Renaud to sea on 22 October: "Concerned by food shortages and a rebellious slave population the French naval commander Jean-Marie Renaud led his small squadron comprising frigates Cybèle and Prudente and three smaller vessels to drive off the British squadron." The Bali Strait article says the decree was read in Paris the same way — the squadron of 1796 was sent "In response to British activity in the region and the reluctance of the inhabitants of Île de France to follow orders from the National Convention abolishing slavery." Precondition-of and not caused: both articles are plain that what provoked the action was the arrival of the British blockade, and that the revolution is the condition the colony and its squadron were in when it arrived.
explanations.french-revolution--battle-of-martinique-: The Martinique article states the motive and the timing together: "The British government was contacted by French planter Louis-François Dubuc, who wished to place Martinique under British protection as the Republic's National Constituent Assembly was about to pass legislation which would abolish slavery in the French colonial empire; the legislation was passed the day before the British invasion of Martinique commenced." It adds that a fortnight later "the British signed the Whitehall Accord on 9 February with counter-revolutionary French planters, which allowed them to keep their chattel property". The French Revolution article carries the other side of the same date: "The Convention voted for the abolition of slavery in the colonies on 4 February 1794 and decreed that all residents of the colonies had the full rights of French citizens irrespective of colour", and, two sentences later, "Martinique remained under British occupation". Reacted to, and in that direction: the planters' handover and the invasion it invited are an answer to what the Revolution was about to do to slavery in the colonies, which is what both articles say, and neither says the Revolution ordered or caused a British expedition.
explanations.french-revolution--haitian-revolution-17: The English article states the link in its own words under "Lasting change": "The Enlightenment ideals and the initiation of the French Revolution were enough to inspire the Haitian Revolution, which evolved into the most successful and comprehensive slave rebellion in history", and in the sentence before it, "The call for modification of society was influenced by the revolution in France, but once the hope for change found a place in the hearts of the Haitian people, there was no stopping the radical reformation that was occurring." The section "Effects of the French Revolution" carries the same claim in detail: the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen "declar[ed] all men free and equal" and was "ambiguous as to whether this equality applied to women, slaves, or citizens of the colonies, and thus influenced the desire for freedom and equality in Saint-Domingue." The type is `inspired` because that is the verb the article uses and the limit of what it asserts: the same section says "The Revolution in Haiti did not wait on the Revolution in France", which is the article refusing the stronger claim. Probable, because the warrant is Wikipedia and not a historian's argument; Wikidata carries no causal statement between Q6534 and Q689128 at all, so this edge has one author where the rest of this branch's have two.
explanations.french-revolution--napoleonic-wars--enab: The article on the Napoleonic Wars opens by saying where they came from: **"The wars originated in political forces arising from the French Revolution (1789–1799) and French Revolutionary Wars (1792–1802) and produced a period of French domination over continental Europe."** Originating in political forces arising from a revolution is enabling and not causing — the sentence names no act of the revolution that set a war going — and the weaker of the two types the source allows is the one written. The same lead lists the Peninsular War among the seven conflicts the Napoleonic Wars are made of, which is why that war is filed under this one rather than linked to it. Probable, for the reason every edge drawn from this source is.
explanations.french-revolution--venezuelan-war-of-ind: The war’s own article names the French Revolution as one of the two things that formed the men who led the movement, which is what "inspired" is for and not more than that: an example followed, not a cause. The article reads: "Persons such as Francisco de Miranda, a long-term Venezuelan expatriate, and Simón Bolívar, a young, Criollo aristocrat-both influenced by Age of Enlightenment ideas and the example of the French Revolution-led the movement."
explanations.great-siege-of-gibraltar--action-of-16-m: The Spanish frigate was off Cape Spartel because of the siege, which the article states as the reason she was there at all: the Santa Catalina “was part of a squadron keeping lookout for any relief convoys heading into Gibraltar, which was then under siege.” A blockade is why two frigates met in the Strait, so `precondition-of`; the siege did not cause this particular action and the article claims no more than the station. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.great-siege-of-gibraltar--action-of-8-ja: The convoy was taken by a fleet that was at sea because of the siege: "Rodney's fleet was en route to relieve Gibraltar, and this action took place several days before Rodney's engagement" off Cape St Vincent. Enabled and not caused: the siege is why a British fleet was off Finisterre in January 1780, not why it met that particular Spanish convoy. The arrow runs this way because the siege had been under way since June 1779 and the action is a step of its first relief.
explanations.haitian-revolution-1791-1804--the-cuban-: The cited account is direct: after the end of slavery in Saint-Domingue at the turn of the nineteenth century, with the Haitian Revolution, Cuba became the most substantial sugar plantation colony in the Caribbean, outperforming the British islands. The richest producer in the world stopped producing and the market went to the island next to it. The revolution’s second effect on Cuba runs the other way and is in the same sources: the white upper class was so afraid of following Haiti that it supported Spanish rule intensely, which is part of why Cuba was still a slave colony of Spain when its neighbours had been republics for two generations.
explanations.insurrection-of-10-august-1792--executio: The execution's own § Background opens on the insurrection: "Following the attack on the Tuileries Palace during the insurrection of 10 August 1792, King Louis XVI was imprisoned at the Temple Prison in Paris, along with his wife Marie Antoinette, their two children and his younger sister Élisabeth." The imprisonment is the article's stated consequence of the insurrection, and it is the state the king was tried and executed in. `precondition-of`: the insurrection did not order the execution, it put the king where the Convention could try him.
explanations.invasion-of-dominica-1778--capture-of-st: St Lucia's article says in its own words what the British expedition was an answer to: "Britain's actions followed the capture of the British-controlled island of Dominica by French forces in a surprise invasion in September 1778." Reacted-to and not caused: the article puts the one after the other and calls it a following, without claiming the loss of Dominica compelled the choice of St Lucia.
explanations.invasion-of-minorca-1781--treaty-of-pari: Minorca's article carries the whole argument: "an important step in the achievement of Spain's aims in its alliance with France against Britain during the American Revolutionary War. The ultimate result was the devolution of the island to Spain in the Treaty of Paris in 1783." Precondition-of: the island had to be taken before it could be ceded.
explanations.invasion-of-the-cape-colony--action-of-9: The Cape article states what the capture was for and what was done with it: "Elphinstone's substantial squadron remained on station at the Cape to deter efforts to recapture the colony. Parts of this force were subsequently deployed to bolster British forces in the Indian Ocean." The February article shows that squadron at work and the colony as its base: Prudente "sailed to the region to the east of the British held Cape Colony to prey on transoceanic merchant shipping sailing to and from Cape Town", and after the action "Ball conducted hasty repairs and then brought the captured Prudente into Table Bay on 15 February. There the captured ship was condemned by the port commander Captain George Losack." Enabled and not caused: a British Cape is what put a British frigate on that coast and gave it somewhere to take a prize; neither article says the 1795 expedition brought on the 1799 encounter.
explanations.invasion-of-the-cape-colony--battle-of-p: The Cape article names the blockade among the capture's consequences: "Parts of this force were subsequently deployed to bolster British forces in the Indian Ocean. The blockade of Île de France was restored." The Port Louis article is the blockade closing: "Returning to Île de France in December, l'Hermite steered for Port Louis but was intercepted by the British blockade squadron, comprising the 74-gun ship of the line HMS Tremendous under John Osborn and the 50-gun HMS Adamant under William Hotham." The Cape is also where the pursuit of Preneuse was run from — "messages to this effect were hastily sent to the commander at the Cape, Captain George Losack who sent the 50-gun HMS Jupiter in pursuit". Enabled: the station the capture created is what made a permanent blockade of Île de France possible, and the articles say so without saying the expedition caused this engagement.
explanations.macau-incident-1799--battle-of-port-loui: The Port Louis article states the consequence of the Macau failure in its own words: "This combined force then attacked an East India Company convoy gathering in the Pearl River in January 1799, but in the ensuing Macau Incident they were driven off by the Royal Navy escort squadron. Dispirited, Sercey returned westwards to Île de France, narrowly avoiding an unequal battle with a large British squadron blockading the port. On arrival he discovered that Preneuse and Brûle-Gueule were the only ships remaining of his original command, the others having returned to France or been lost in battle." That return is what brought Preneuse back under the blockade of Port Louis, and it is what "In September 1799 Sercey dispersed his remaining ships" follows from. Precondition-of and not caused: being driven off at Macau did not order the December cruise, it put the last frigate back where the blockade was.
explanations.new-york-and-new-jersey-campaign--battle: The Trenton article, at revision 1377458911, names the campaign as the reason the attack was attempted at all: “The Continental Army had previously suffered several defeats in New York and had been forced to retreat through New Jersey to Pennsylvania. Morale in the army was low; to end the year on a positive note, George Washington, Commander-in-Chief of the Continental Army, devised a plan to cross the Delaware River on the night of December 25–26 and surround the Hessians’ garrison.” The words “suffered several defeats” carry the article's own link to the campaign, so the cause the sentence names is the campaign and not one of its battles. The campaign article, at revision 1370629551, supplies the other half — the target the campaign had left exposed: “Howe ordered his troops into winter quarters in December, establishing a chain of outposts from New York City to Burlington, New Jersey”, and, in its account of the counterattack, “While worrying over how to hold his army together, Washington organized attacks on the relatively exposed British outposts. German commanders Carl von Donop and Johann Rall, whose brigades were at the end of the chain of outposts, were frequent targets of these raids.” Motive and target both come from the campaign, which is why this is `caused`. The campaign is filed under `american-revolutionary-war` and so is Trenton — both from their own `P361`, which is `Q40949` for each — so this edge runs between siblings and A14's parent-to-child bar does not reach it. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.north-channel-naval-duel--battle-of-flam: The Ranger's action is where the campaign Flamborough Head ends began: "it was the first American naval success within Atlantic waters... The action was one of a series of actions by Jones that brought the war to British waters." Flamborough Head, off Yorkshire fifteen months later, is the last and most celebrated of that series, and the same officer commands both. Precondition-of and not caused: the article makes the one a member of a series, not the cause of another action in it.
explanations.rebellion-of-tupac-amaru-ii--siege-of-cu: The article gives the march on Cusco as a move the rising made out of its own position, and gives the reason in one sentence: **"Seeking to maintain the advantages gained at Quiquijana, Sangarará, and Lampa, he decided to anticipate the enemy and go on the offensive."** The sentence before it says what he was anticipating — **"Túpac Amaru had received news of an impending attack on Tinta, which was why he quickly returned to Tungasuca"** — and the one after it that "the rebel leader began preparations for the great expedition against Cusco", the army departing on 20 December with some five thousand armed men. This is an edge from an umbrella to one of its own parts, written because `parent` is a display fact that never enters the adjacency: the three months of rising that put an army outside Cusco are the argument, and without this edge the graph could not walk it. `enabled` and not `caused`: the article gives the decision to Túpac Amaru and a warning about Tinta, not to the rising as such. Walker is the work the article itself cites through this stretch; it is cited and not read, which is why the confidence stays `probable`.
explanations.rebellion-of-tupac-amaru-ii--spanish-ame: The wars' article, under "Background", names this rising among the revolts the Bourbon reforms provoked: **"In other areas, the changes in the crown's economic and administrative policies led to tensions with locals, which at times erupted into open revolts, such as the Revolt of the Comuneros in New Granada and the Rebellion of Túpac Amaru II in Peru."** The next paragraph is what this edge is drawn from and it is equivocal, so it is quoted whole: **"The loss of high offices to peninsulars and the eighteenth-century revolts in Spanish South America were some of the direct causes of the wars of independence, which took place decades later, but they have been considered important elements of the political background in which the wars took place."** `precondition-of` is the weakest type that sentence supports, and `caused` is not written from a sentence that hedges itself in its own second clause. The paragraph cites Lynch, Rodríguez and Kinsbruner; the one the article gives in full is cited here beside it, and it is cited and not read, which is why the confidence stays probable.
explanations.revolt-of-cairo--siege-of-el-arish--enab: The El Arish article opens its Background with the connection in one clause of its own: "Napoleon had recently subdued a revolt against the French occupation in Egypt, and with his borders secure, continued his offensive against the Ottoman Empire." Enabled and not caused: putting down the rising in Cairo did not make the march into Syria necessary, it made it possible — the article's "with his borders secure" is the whole of the mechanism it claims, and the offensive it describes was already Bonaparte's intention.
explanations.revolt-of-the-comuneros-new-granada--spa: The same paragraph of the wars' article that names the Túpac Amaru rising names this one in the same breath — **"open revolts, such as the Revolt of the Comuneros in New Granada and the Rebellion of Túpac Amaru II in Peru"** — and the same hedged sentence follows it: **"The loss of high offices to peninsulars and the eighteenth-century revolts in Spanish South America were some of the direct causes of the wars of independence, which took place decades later, but they have been considered important elements of the political background in which the wars took place."** The revolt's own article gives the grievance: the rising was "in reaction to the increase in taxation to raise funds for the defense of the region against the British and a rise in the price of tobacco and brandy", which "were part of the late eighteenth-century Bourbon Reforms" (revision 1369393858). `precondition-of` for the same reason as its twin, and probable for the same reason.
explanations.siege-of-acre-1799--battle-of-mount-tabo: Mount Tabor's own lead states the chain without a gap: "Upon hearing that an Ottoman army had been sent from Damascus to Acre for the purpose of forcing the French to raise the siege, Bonaparte sent out detachments to track it down. Kléber led his division of 2,000 men and decided to engage the Ottoman army near Mount Tabor." The siege is why the army from Damascus was on the road and why Bonaparte sent men after it; caused rather than enabled, because the article gives the relief of Acre as the purpose of the march the battle intercepted. Probable and not consensus: this is Wikipedia's account of the campaign, not a work it cites for the point (A2).
explanations.siege-of-boston--battle-of-bunker-hill--: The battle was fought because both sides reached for the same unoccupied hills, and both articles say so in the same words. The Boston article, at revision 1377282932, gives the British plan and the answer to it: “The British plan was to fortify Bunker Hill and Dorchester Heights. They fixed the date for taking Dorchester Heights at June 18, but the colonists’ committee of safety learned of the British plans on June 15. In response, they sent instructions to General Ward to fortify Bunker Hill and the heights of Charlestown.” The Bunker Hill article, at revision 1375011142, arrives at it from the other side — “the leaders of the colonial forces besieging Boston learned that the British were planning to send troops out from the city to fortify the unoccupied hills surrounding the city … In response, 1,200 colonial troops under the command of William Prescott stealthily occupied Bunker Hill and Breed’s Hill” — and it is that fortification the British attacked on 17 June. Read in the atlas’s direction, `A reacted-to B` says B answered A: the siege stands at the `from` end and the battle at the `to`. The two records are siblings under `american-revolutionary-war` and not parent and child, so A14 does not reach this edge. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.siege-of-brimstone-hill--battle-of-saint: The fleet action was fought over the siege: "The Comte de Grasse, who delivered de Bouille's troops and supported the siege, was outmanoeuvred and deprived of his anchorage by Admiral Samuel Hood... Hood's attempts to relieve the ongoing siege were unsuccessful, and the garrison capitulated after one month." Precondition-of: the siege is what Hood came to lift and what de Grasse was covering.
explanations.siege-of-brimstone-hill--treaty-of-paris: The island taken in 1782 is one of the things the peace had to settle: "About a year later, the Treaty of Paris restored Saint Kitts and adjacent Nevis to British rule." Precondition-of and not caused: the capture is what gave the treaty something to restore, and the article says only that.
